<problem>
Let \(S^1=\{z\in\mathbb C:|z|=1\}\). A stable complex structure on a closed smooth real \(2n\)-manifold \(M\) means a complex vector-bundle structure \(J\) on
\[
E=TM\oplus(M\times\mathbb R^{2k})
\]
for some integer \(k\ge0\). Here closed means compact without boundary. For a smooth \(S^1\)-action on \(M\), require that its derivative action on \(TM\), extended by the trivial action on the stabilizing \(\mathbb R^{2k}\) fibers, commute with \(J\). Orient \(M\) using the complex orientation of \((E,J)\) and the standard orientation of the stabilizing real summand, and write \(c_j(M,J)=c_j(E,J)\).

Define \(\mathcal E\) to be the set of even integers \(2n\ge16\) for which there exist such an \(M\), an invariant stable complex structure \(J\), and a smooth \(S^1\)-action satisfying both of the following conditions:

1. The set \(M^{S^1}=\{p\in M:z\cdot p=p\text{ for every }z\in S^1\}\) consists of exactly four isolated points.
2. At least one Chern number
\[
\left\langle c_{i_1}(M,J)\cdots c_{i_r}(M,J),[M]\right\rangle,
\qquad r\ge1,\quad i_j\ge1,\quad i_1+\cdots+i_r=n,
\]
is nonzero.

Manifolds may be disconnected, and actions need not be effective. Determine \(\mathcal E\) explicitly.
</problem>

A complete answer to this problem: A complete answer must specify the set \(\mathcal E\) exactly, by an explicit list or an explicit membership rule for every even integer \(2n\ge16\). It must establish existence in every included dimension and nonexistence in every excluded dimension.

7	In particular, the answer is different from what one would obtain by imposing an almost complex structure rather than a stable complex structure. The 18-dimensional examples below have \(\chi_y=0\), but have a nonzero Chern number.
8	
9	I give a computer-assisted proof. The computations are exact computations over \(\mathbb Q\), not numerical searches. Importantly, the exclusion of arbitrarily large dimensions is reduced to polynomial-ideal certificates with the dimension as an indeterminate.
10	
11	## 1. Fixed-point formulas and a small Chern-number algebra
12	
13	Write the complex tangent weights at a fixed point \(p\) as
14	\[
15	w_{p,1},\ldots,w_{p,n}\in\mathbb Z\setminus\{0\}.
16	\]
17	The stabilizing summand contributes only zero weights. Let \(\epsilon_p\in\{1,-1\}\) compare the orientation in the question with the orientation of the nonzero complex weight spaces. Put
18	\[
19	a_{p,j}=e_j(w_{p,1},\ldots,w_{p,n}),\qquad
20	b_p=\frac{\epsilon_p}{\prod_iw_{p,i}}.
21	\]
22	
23	We use the usual equivariant cohomology localization formula and equivariant index formula. These apply to invariant stable complex structures, with precisely the signs \(\epsilon_p\).
24	
25	### A Chern-number algebra of dimension at most four
26	
27	Give \(R=\mathbb Q[c_1,c_2,\ldots]\) the grading \(\deg c_j=j\). Let
28	\[
29	\varphi:R_n\longrightarrow\mathbb Q
30	\]
31	be evaluation as a Chern number of \(M\). Assume that \(\varphi\ne0\).
32	
33	Define its graded annihilator by
34	\[
35	I_d=\{f\in R_d:\varphi(fg)=0\text{ for every }g\in R_{n-d}\},
36	\]
37	and set \(A=R/I\), with degrees above \(n\) killed. Then \(A\) is a graded Poincaré-duality algebra with \(A_0=A_n=\mathbb Q\).
38	
39	Here is the useful fixed-point bound:
40	\[
41	\dim_{\mathbb Q}A\le4.                                      \tag{1}
42	\]
43	
44	Indeed, evaluate Chern polynomials at the four vectors
45	\((a_{p,1},a_{p,2},\ldots)\), and let \(F_d\subseteq\mathbb Q^4\) be the span of evaluations of polynomials of weighted degree at most \(d\). Localization says
46	\[
47	\sum_p b_p f(a_p)=0\qquad(\deg f<n).
48	\]
49	Consequently, if a homogeneous \(f\in R_d\) evaluates into \(F_{d-1}\), then
50	\[
51	\varphi(fg)=0\qquad(g\in R_{n-d}).
52	\]
53	Thus \(A\) is a quotient of the associated graded algebra of \(F_\bullet\), proving (1).
54	
55	Classification of such small graded Poincaré-duality algebras is elementary. Because there is only one Chern generator in each degree, their possible positive degrees are
56	\[
57	\{n\},\qquad \{a,n\}\ (n=2a),\qquad
58	\{a,b,n\}\ (a+b=n).
59	\]
60	In the last case the only possible extra power is when \(b=2a\).
61	
62	It follows that, for some \(a\le b\), \(a+b=n\), **all Chern numbers vanish except possibly**
63	\[
64	c_n,\quad c_ac_b,                                           \tag{2}
65	\]
66	with the additional possibility
67	\[
68	c_a^3\quad\text{when }n=3a.                                 \tag{3}
69	\]
70	The case in which only \(c_n\) can be nonzero can be included in (2) by assigning zero to the other number.
71	
72	## 2. The restriction supplied by the \(\chi_y\)-genus
73	
74	Define \(q_k(y)\) by
75	\[
76	\log\left(\frac{Q_y(z)}{1+y}\right)
77	 =\sum_{k\ge1}q_k(y)z^k,\qquad
78	Q_y(z)=\frac{z(1+ye^{-z})}{1-e^{-z}}.
79	\]
80	If
81	\[
82	s=\frac{1-y}{1+y},
83	\]
84	then
85	\[
86	\frac{Q_y(z)}{1+y}
87	 =\frac z2\coth\frac z2+\frac{sz}{2}.                         \tag{4}
88	\]
89	In particular the \(q_k\) are polynomials in \(s\).
90	
91	Newton identities, together with (2)–(3), show that
92	\[
93	\chi_y(M)\in (1+y)^n
94	 \operatorname{span}_{\mathbb Q}\{q_n,q_aq_b\},               \tag{5}
95	\]
96	with \(q_a^3\) added when \(n=3a\). Before substituting the particular polynomials \(q_k\), the change from the Chern numbers in (2)–(3) to the coefficients in (5) is triangular with nonzero diagonal. Thus linear independence of these polynomials implies that \(\chi_y=0\) forces all the Chern numbers to vanish.
97	
98	For completeness, the rigidity needed here follows directly from the equivariant index formula. It expresses the equivariant genus as
99	\[
100	\sum_p\epsilon_p
101	 \prod_i\frac{1+yt^{w_{p,i}}}{1-t^{w_{p,i}}}.
102	\]
103	Its coefficients are Laurent polynomials in \(t\); the displayed expression is bounded at both \(0\) and \(\infty\). It is therefore constant in \(t\).
104	
105	Put
106	\[
107	H(x)=\chi_{-x}(M).
108	\]
109	Taking the two limits gives
110	\[
111	H(x)=\sum_p\epsilon_p x^{d_p},
112	\qquad H(x)=x^nH(x^{-1}),                                   \tag{6}
113	\]
114	where \(d_p\) counts negative weights. Hence \(H\) is reciprocal, has integer coefficients, and has coefficient \(\ell^1\)-norm at most four.
115	
116	Moreover, its middle coefficient, if present, is even: \(H(1)=\sum_p\epsilon_p\) is even, and the other coefficients occur in pairs. Consequently every nonzero possibility in (6) is either one signed polynomial
117	\[
118	x^i+x^{n-i},
119	\]
120	or a sum of two such signed polynomials, repetitions allowed.
121	
122	Equivalently,
123	\[
124	G(t)=e^{-nt/2}H(e^t)
125	\]
126	is a sum of at most two signed terms \(2\cosh(\xi t)\). Thus, writing
127	\[
128	M_j=G^{(2j)}(0),
129	\]
130	the Hankel matrix
131	\[
132	(M_{i+j})_{0\le i\le2,\ 0\le j\le4}                         \tag{7}
133	\]
134	has rank at most two.
135	
136	These restrictions will exclude every \(n\ge8\), except \(n=9\).
137	
138	## 3. Excluding all \(n\ge15\)
139	
140	This part is uniform in \(n\).
141	
142	Set
143	\[
144	U(t)=\frac{2\sinh(t/2)}t,\qquad L(t)=\log U(t),
145	\qquad r_k(t)=-kt^kq_k(-e^t).
146	\]
147	A direct expansion of the logarithm defining \(q_k\) gives
148	\[
149	q_k(-e^t)
150	=-\frac1{kt^k}
151	 +\frac{(-1)^kL^{(k)}(t)-L^{(k)}(0)}{k!}.                  \tag{8}
152	\]
153	In particular \(r_k(0)=1\). Its first nonconstant term is
154	\[
155	\begin{cases}
156	\displaystyle
157	\frac{B_{k+1}}{(k+1)(k-1)!}\,t^{k+1},&k\text{ odd},\\[6pt]
158	\displaystyle
159	-\frac{B_{k+2}}{2(k+2)(k-1)!}\,t^{k+2},&k\text{ even}.
160	\end{cases}                                               \tag{9}
161	\]
162	All these coefficients are nonzero.
163	
164	Let
165	\[
166	\kappa=G(0)=\langle c_n,[M]\rangle\in\{-4,-2,0,2,4\}.
167	\]
168	
169	### 3.1. The case \(\kappa\ne0\)
170	
171	Changing all signs, suppose \(\kappa>0\).
172	
173	If the smaller degree \(a\) in (2) is at least four, (8)–(9) imply
174	\[
175	G(t)=\kappa U(t)^n+O(t^6).
176	\]
177	The same holds for the cubic case \(n=3a\), \(a\ge5\). Therefore
178	\[
179	\frac{G''(0)}{\kappa}=\frac n{12},\qquad
180	\frac{G^{(4)}(0)}{\kappa}=\frac{n(5n-2)}{240}.              \tag{10}
181	\]
182	
183	If \(\kappa=2\), (6) implies \(G=2\cosh(\xi t)\). Equations (10) would require
184	\[
185	\xi^2=\frac n{12},\qquad
186	\xi^4=\frac{n(5n-2)}{240},
187	\]
188	which give \(n=3/5\).
189	
190	If \(\kappa=4\), we have
191	\[
192	G=2\cosh(\xi t)+2\cosh(\eta t).
193	\]
194	Equations (10) give
195	\[
196	\xi^2+\eta^2=\frac n6,\qquad
197	\xi^4+\eta^4=\frac{n(5n-2)}{120}.
198	\]
199	But \(\xi^4+\eta^4\le(\xi^2+\eta^2)^2\), whereas the required difference is
200	\[
201	\frac{n(5n-2)}{120}-\frac{n^2}{36}
202	=\frac{n(5n-6)}{360}>0.
203	\]
204	This is impossible.
205	
206	It remains to handle \(a=1,2,3\) in (2). Since \(n\ge15\), \(b=n-a\ge12\). Formula (8) then gives, through degree twelve,
207	\[
208	G(t)=U(t)^n\bigl(\kappa+\lambda R_a(t)\bigr)+O(t^{14}),      \tag{11}
209	\]
210	where
211	\[
212	\begin{aligned}
213	R_1&=\frac t2\coth(t/2)-1,\\
214	R_2&=\frac{t^2}{4\sinh^2(t/2)}+\frac{t^2}{12}-1,\\
215	R_3&=\frac{t^3\cosh(t/2)}{8\sinh^3(t/2)}-1.
216	\end{aligned}                                             \tag{12}
217	\]
218	
219	Normalize \(\kappa=1\) by dividing \(G\) by \(\kappa\), and put \(h=\lambda/\kappa\). Compute the moments through degree twelve from
220	\[
221	U(t)^n(1+hR_a(t)).
222	\]
223	The \(3\times3\) minors of (7) must vanish. Exact polynomial-ideal calculation gives the following certificates:
224	\[
225	\begin{array}{c|c}
226	a&\text{polynomial belonging to the ideal of those minors}\\ \hline
227	1&n^2(n-1)^2\\
228	2&n^2(n-2)^2\\
229	3&n^2(n-3)^2.
230	\end{array}                                               \tag{13}
231	\]
232	The code below computes and verifies these ideal-membership assertions. None is compatible with \(n\ge15\).
233	
234	### 3.2. The case \(\kappa=0\)
235	
236	Except possibly when \(a=1\), (8)–(9) give \(G(t)=O(t^4)\). But a nonzero polynomial with at most four monomials cannot have a nonzero root of multiplicity four: its first four derivative equations form a Vandermonde system in the four exponents. Thus
237	\[
238	\chi_y(M)=0.                                               \tag{14}
239	\]
240	
241	When \(a=1\), (11) becomes
242	\[
243	G(t)=\lambda U(t)^nR_1(t)+O(t^{14}).
244	\]
245	If \(\lambda=0\), the Chern numbers vanish. Otherwise divide by \(\lambda\). The ideal of the minors (7), now calculated from \(U^nR_1\), is the unit ideal. This is another exact certificate verified below. Hence this case is impossible.
246	
247	We must check that (14) forces the Chern numbers to vanish.
248	
249	For the two-generator span in (5), a dependence would require
250	\[
251	r_n=r_ar_b.
252	\]
253	Using (9), the first nonconstant term on the right cannot cancel, except potentially when \(a\) is even and \(b=a+1\). In that case its coefficient is proportional to
254	\[
255	-\frac12+\frac1a,
256	\]
257	which vanishes only for \((a,b)=(2,3)\), not for \(n\ge15\). Thus the two polynomials are independent.
258	
259	For the cubic case \(n=3d\), \(d\ge5\), normalize a putative dependence to
260	\[
261	A r_{3d}+B r_dr_{2d}+C r_d^3=0.
262	\]
263	The constant and first nonconstant terms give
264	\[
265	A+B+C=0,\qquad B+3C=0.
266	\]
267	If \(d\) is even, the first term of \(r_{2d}-1\), in degree \(2d+2\), forces \(B=0\), and then all coefficients vanish.
268	
269	If \(d\) is odd, let \(u\) and \(v\) be the leading coefficients of \(r_d-1\) and \(r_{2d}-1\). The degree \(2d+2\) equation gives
270	\[
271	C(u^2-v)=0.
272	\]
273	The Bernoulli-number formula yields
274	\[
275	\frac v{u^2}
276	=\frac{2d+1}{2d}\frac{\zeta(2d+2)}{\zeta(d+1)^2}>1
277	\qquad(d\ge5).
278	\]
279	Here is an elementary bound proving the strict inequality:
280	\[
281	\zeta(d+1)-1
282	<\frac{d+2}{d\,2^{d+1}}\le\frac1{8d},
283	\]
284	so \(\zeta(d+1)^2<1+1/(2d)\), while \(\zeta(2d+2)>1\).
285	Thus again the polynomials are independent.
286	
287	This proves that **no \(n\ge15\) is possible**.
288	
289	## 4. The remaining finite calculation: \(8\le n\le14\)
290	
291	For each \(n\) and \(1\le a\le n/2\), form the coefficient matrix of
292	\[
293	(1-x)^nq_n,\qquad (1-x)^nq_aq_{n-a},
294	\]
295	and, if \(n=3a\), also \((1-x)^nq_a^3\), after substituting
296	\[
297	s=\frac{1+x}{1-x}.
298	\]
299	
300	There are only 37 matrices. The code below verifies, over \(\mathbb Q\), that:
301	
302	* no nonzero signed sum of at most two reciprocal pairs \(x^i+x^{n-i}\) belongs to any of these column spaces;
303	* every matrix has independent columns except the one for \((n,a)=(9,3)\).
304	
305	The exceptional dependence is
306	\[
307	q_9+3q_3q_6+\frac32q_3^3=0.                                \tag{15}
308	\]
309	
310	By Sections 1–2, every manifold in the question must pass these tests. Therefore the only remaining dimension is
311	\[
312	2n=18.                                                     \tag{16}
313	\]
314	
315	This argument used neither connectedness nor effectiveness.
316	
317	## 5. Constructing an 18-dimensional example
318	
319	We now prove that the exceptional dimension actually occurs.
320	
321	Use the standard homogeneous almost complex sphere
322	\[
323	S^6=G_2/SU(3).
324	\]
325	For the circle in the maximal torus specified by the triple
326	\[
327	(a,b,-a-b),
328	\]
329	the sphere has exactly two fixed points, with tangent weights
330	\[
331	(a,b,-a-b),\qquad (-a,-b,a+b),
332	\]
333	provided all three entries are nonzero.
334	
335	Choose
336	\[
337	\alpha=(1,9,-10),\qquad \beta=(5,6,-11).
338	\]
339	They satisfy
340	\[
341	e_1(\alpha)=e_1(\beta)=0,\qquad
342	e_2(\alpha)=e_2(\beta)=-91,
343	\]
344	but
345	\[
346	e_3(\alpha)=-90,\qquad e_3(\beta)=-330.                     \tag{17}
347	\]
348	
349	### An equivariant clutching map
350	
351	Let \(\phi_\alpha,\phi_\beta:S^1\to G_2\) be these homomorphisms. The two induced \(G_2\)-bundles over \(\mathbb CP^5\) become isomorphic after replacing both homomorphisms by
352	\[
353	z\longmapsto\phi_\alpha(z^N),\qquad
354	z\longmapsto\phi_\beta(z^N)
355	\]
356	for some positive integer \(N\).
357	
358	Here are the obstruction-theoretic details. The only nonfinite homotopy group of \(BG_2\) in degrees at most eleven is
359	\[
360	\pi_4(BG_2)\cong\mathbb Z;
361	\]
362	rationally its next generator is in degree twelve. The degree-four characteristic class of the induced bundles is proportional to
363	\[
364	(a^2+ab+b^2)x^2.
365	\]
366	Both pairs in (17) give \(91x^2\), so this obstruction agrees integrally. All remaining obstructions to a homotopy of their classifying maps on \(\mathbb CP^5\) have finite coefficient groups.
367	
368	The power map
369	\[
370	[z_0:\cdots:z_5]\longmapsto[z_0^N:\cdots:z_5^N]
371	\]
372	acts on \(H^{2j}(\mathbb CP^5;A)\) as multiplication by \(N^j\). Successively choosing multiples of the exponents of the finitely many obstruction groups kills all the obstructions. Iterating power maps is again a power map. This proves the asserted isomorphism.
373	
374	Equivalently, there is a smooth equivariant clutching map
375	\[
376	S^{11}\longrightarrow G_2
377	\]
378	for the free scalar circle action on \(S^{11}\subset\mathbb C^6\), with the two fiber actions \(\phi_{N\alpha}\) and \(\phi_{N\beta}\).
379	
380	Clutch across the equator of
381	\[
382	S^{12}=S(\mathbb C^6\oplus\mathbb R).
383	\]
384	We obtain an equivariant principal \(G_2\)-bundle \(P\to S^{12}\), and set
385	\[
386	M=P\times_{G_2}S^6.
387	\]
388	This is a closed, connected, smooth 18-manifold.
389	
390	The base circle action has two fixed points, and over each the fiber action has two fixed points. Thus \(M\) has exactly four fixed points.
391	
392	### The invariant stable complex structure
393	
394	The vertical tangent bundle has its \(G_2\)-invariant complex structure. Also
395	\[
396	TS^{12}\oplus\mathbb R^2
397	\]
398	has an invariant complex structure coming from
399	\(\mathbb C^6\oplus\mathbb C\). An invariant horizontal distribution therefore supplies the required complex structure on
400	\[
401	TM\oplus\mathbb R^2.
402	\]
403	The stabilizing fibers have trivial circle action, as required in the question.
404	
405	Nonequivariantly, the stabilized base bundle is complex trivial. Furthermore \(H^2(M)=H^4(M)=0\). If \(V\) denotes the vertical complex rank-three bundle, then
406	\[
407	c(M)=c(V)=1+c_3(V).
408	\]
409	Thus the only possibly nonzero Chern number is \(c_3^3\).
410	
411	The four fixed-point weight lists and signs are
412	\[
413	\begin{array}{c|c}
414	\text{weights}&\epsilon\\ \hline
415	1,1,1,1,1,1,\ N\alpha&+1\\
416	1,1,1,1,1,1,-N\alpha&+1\\
417	1,1,1,1,1,1,\ N\beta&-1\\
418	1,1,1,1,1,1,-N\beta&-1.
419	\end{array}                                               \tag{18}
420	\]
421	The signs are opposite at the two base poles.
422	
423	Put
424	\[
425	K=20-546N^2,\qquad D_\alpha=-90N^3,\qquad D_\beta=-330N^3.
426	\]
427	At the two points over either pole, the third equivariant Chern class is \(K\pm D\), and the Euler denominator is \(\pm D\). Localization gives
428	\[
429	\begin{aligned}
430	\langle c_3^3,[M]\rangle
431	&=\left(\frac{(K+D_\alpha)^3-(K-D_\alpha)^3}{D_\alpha}\right)\\
432	&\quad-\left(\frac{(K+D_\beta)^3-(K-D_\beta)^3}{D_\beta}\right)\\
433	&=2(D_\alpha^2-D_\beta^2)\\
434	&=\boxed{-201600N^6}\ne0.                                  \tag{19}
435	\end{aligned}
436	\]
437	Hence \(18\in\mathcal E\).
438	
439	## 6. Executable exact verification
440	
441	This is the complete verification script. It checks the 37 finite cases, computes the dimension-independent ideal certificates, and checks every Chern-number localization calculation for (18), symbolically for all \(N\).
442	
443	```python
444	import sympy as S
445	from itertools import combinations
446	from functools import lru_cache
447	from math import prod
448	
449	# I. Exact finite check: complex dimensions 8,...,14.
450	s, x = S.symbols('s x')
451	q = {}
452	Ac = [S.S.One, s/2] + [
453	    S.bernoulli(j)/S.factorial(j) if j % 2 == 0 else S.S.Zero
454	    for j in range(2, 15)
455	]
456	# If A(z)=1+sum A_j z^j and log A(z)=sum q_j z^j,
457	# j A_j = sum_{i=1}^j i q_i A_{j-i}.
458	for j in range(1, 15):
459	    q[j] = S.expand(
460	        Ac[j] - sum(S.Rational(i, j)*q[i]*Ac[j-i]
461	                    for i in range(1, j))
462	    )
463	
464	kernels = []
